title: Design against crime
titleCn: 设计防犯罪：产品与环境如何防盗

paragraphs.text: Section four. You will hear a design student giving a presentation about how crime can be prevented through improving products and environments.
First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

In my presentation today, I'm going to talk about how we can look at crime prevention in a new way, through designing products and environments so that thieves and other offenders will actually be less likely to commit crimes, either because there are fewer opportunities or fewer inducements.

Now, although this is a relatively new concept here in Britain, what we call situational crime prevention started in the USA as early as the nineteen seventies. But it's generally agreed that the need for this approach is growing very rapidly, in particular because of advances in technology, which mean most of us carry around many more things which are temptations to thieves.
Nowadays, in a single bag we carry around with us, we may have numerous costly objects and also a lot of personal information which can, with ingenuity, be used or, should I say, abused by criminals.
So what can we do to make life easier for ourselves and more difficult for thieves simply by thinking more carefully about design?
Well, there are really two areas to consider.
Let's look first at the products themselves.

If an object can be picked up easily, a simple way to protect it is to place a phone number on it in such a way that it can't be wiped off. That way, the object can't be sold on to an unsuspecting person.

Another commonly stolen item is bikes. Increasingly, these have security wires or cables, and when these are cut by a thief trying to get to the bike, a lock snaps into place, which means no one can use it.

Historically, of course, the thing most people have wanted to steal is banknotes, and so a lot of ingenious strategies have been developed. For example, if you try to copy a fifty-pound note on a machine, you can't, because the machine has been programmed to detect the security devices in the paper. This idea is also beginning to be adopted by other sectors.

In different parts of the world, designers are experimenting with a variety of anti-shoplifting devices. In Japan, for instance, they have invented a ball which can be thrown at thieves escaping from the shop. This contains fluorescent and offensively smelling stuff which sticks to people and can easily be picked up by police dogs. And in the UK, tags are attached to clothing in shops. When the tag is tampered with, ink is released onto the fabric, meaning the stolen items can't be worn or sold on to someone else. All of which makes it much less attractive for thieves to bother stealing the items in the first place.

Of course, it can take a while for people to realize the value of anti-crime design. Quite a lot of research has been done to find out about practices and attitudes in business. A questionnaire sent out last year generated a number of valuable findings.

Probably the thing that emerged most strongly is that the most powerful driver is when manufacturers recognize that designing products to be crime-resistant is good, profitable business. And it's also the case that products that are properly protected have lower insurance charges. So that's an added incentive.
Let's turn now to the way environments can be designed to prevent crime.

Studies have shown that there are certain places which are particularly susceptible. Bus stops are notoriously bad, as is any form of transport depot. We may not be able to remove the threat entirely, but we can improve the situation in these environments by recognizing certain problematic architectural design features, such as bad lighting. This is something which can be tackled relatively easily, of course.
Another thing which makes problems worse is having areas like corners in which people cannot easily be seen.
Retail spaces, such as shops, are also obvious places where crime is rife. But research has shown that there are quite simple ways to make life difficult for shoplifters.

That is the end of section four.
You now have half a minute to check your answers.
